senses: A wise legislator or lawgiver.
Any legislator.
ety: From Ancient Greek Σόλων (Sólōn), the name of an influential Athenian statesman.

senses: A municipal administrator during the Italian Fascist regime (1927–43).
ety: From Italian podesta, from Latin potestas (“power; powerful one”). Doublet of poustie. See potent.

senses: The first principle of existing things in pre-Socratic philosophy, initially assumed to be of water.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἀρχή (arkhḗ, literally “beginning, origin”).

senses: Among the Huli people of Papua New Guinea, a male warrior who grows his hair long in order to weave it into a ceremonial wig.
One who, or that which, upgrades.
A facility that upgrades bitumen into synthetic crude oil.
Characteristic of an excitotoxin
A building providing sleeping quarters for workers or guests, especially in a rural setting.
A study (room).
Essence, being.
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek οὐσία (ousía), from οὖσα (oûsa), the feminine present participle of εἰμί (eimí, “I am”).

senses: To cause, bring about (an event); to accomplish, to carry out (a wish, plan etc.).
ety: From the participle stem of Renaissance Latin effectuare, or its source, Latin effectus (“effect”); probably after Middle French effectuer.
examples: A military draft derives from Congress’s power to raise armies; federal jury duty effectuates the Sixth Amendment right to a jury trial.

senses: Ether or atmosphere, as one of the elements in Hindu philosophy.
One who has pneumonia.
ety: From the post-Classical Latin pneumonicus and its etymon, the Ancient Greek πνευμονικός (pneumonikós).

senses: A flavored alcoholic beverage that is usually very sweet and contains a high percentage of alcohol.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French liqueur. Doublet of liquor.

senses: A grandfather.
A cobalamin (form of vitamin B₁₂) used to treat neuropathies.
A flavoured frozen dessert of South Asia, made from milk and resembling ice cream.
ety: From Hindi क़ुल्फ़ी (qulfī)/Urdu قلفی (qulfī), from Classical Persian قفلی (quflī) from قفل (qufl), from Arabic قُفْل (qufl, “lock, bolt”).
examples: Vada pav sandwiches and mango kulfi were sold at the concession stand.

senses: A bristlecone pine, of subsection Pinus subsect. Balfourianae.
All the electrical components and wiring of a machine or system.
Someone or something that tempts, especially a man that tempts.
ety: From Middle English tempter, temptere, temptour, temptoure, from Old French tempter, temptere, tenteor, Anglo-Norman tempteour, temptur and Middle English tempten (“to tempt”); equivalent to tempt + -er.
examples: He is a tempter of married women.

senses: An arrangement of siphon tubes for assisting circulation in a liquid.
A person who studies cosmology.
Within the vagina.
An electronic musical instrument that creates its sounds with electronics and generally is played via a keyboard.
An electronic instrument consisting of a module, or a set of modules, that creates its sounds with electronics and does not have any keyboard.
Coconut milk.
The process or practice of ostracizing.
Having an unusual and unattractive shape; deformed, misshapen; hence, hideous, ugly.
ety: From Middle English deforme (“out of shape, deformed”) [and other forms], from Middle French deforme (modern French difforme (“misshapen, deformed”)), or directly from its etymon Latin dēfōrmis (“departing physically from the correct shape, deformed, malformed, misshapen, ugly; (figuratively) departing morally from the correct quality, base, disgraceful, shameful, unbecoming”), from dē- (prefix meaning ‘away from; from’) + fōrma (“form, appearance, figure, shape; fine form, beauty; design, outline, plan; model, pattern; mould, stamp; (figuratively) kind, manner, sort”) (further etymology unkno

senses: Something wrinkly like a prune.
ety: From Middle English prune, from Old French prune, from Vulgar Latin *prūna, feminine singular formed from the neutral plural of Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦνον (proûnon), variant of προῦμνον (proûmnon, “plum”), a loanword from a language of Asia Minor. Doublet of plum.

senses: That which is referenced.
Unsupported.
ety: From Middle English un-fedd, unfedd, equivalent to un- + fed.

senses: A road ascending a slope in Ancient Rome.
An artist who paints miniature figures or scenes.
A person who creates or collects miniature figurines (such as dolls).
examples: Power scissors Every miniaturist should have a pair.
The miniaturist's hobby is as varied as the people who pursue it.
There are many smaller devices to be found, particularly in Scotland, which are more suited to the miniaturist.

senses: The currency of Greece in ancient times and again from 1832 until 2001, with the symbol ₯, since replaced by the euro.
A coin worth one drachma.
An Ancient Greek weight of about 66.5 grains, or 4.3 grams.
A later Greek weight equal to a gram.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin drachma and its etymon Doric Greek δρᾰχμᾱ́ (drăkhmā́). Doublet of dram, diram, dirham, dirhem, adarme, and dam.

senses: Able to ferment or be fermented.
An experimental practice or tendency, especially in the arts
An empirical or pragmatic approach which emphasizes the importance of experimentation
examples: By playing up the lushness of Webern’s “Langsamer Satz” and the experimentalism of Beethoven’s “Serioso” Quartet, for example, they created the impression that Beethoven was the more adventurous composer.
Finally, I argued that moderate experimentalism and IAE can help resolve these different kinds of conflicts.

senses: An ethical code of the samurai that was prevalent in feudal Japan that advocated unquestioning loyalty to the master at all costs and obedience in all deeds, valuing honor above life.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 武(ぶ)士(し)道(どう) (bushidō), from Middle Chinese 武士 (mju^X dzri^X, “warrior”) + 道 (daw^X, “way”). Cognate with Mandarin 武士 (wǔshì) and Cantonese 武士 (mou⁵ si⁶).

senses: The development of sex characteristics that are typically found in men.
To produce an image of the structure or function of part of the brain.
Fried bread.
Synonym of chrism.
The herb chervil.
ety: From Middle English mirre, from Old English myrre, from Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρα (múrrha), from Semitic. Compare Arabic مُرّ (murr, “myrrh”, literally “bitterness”), Hebrew מור / מֹר (mōr, “myrrh”, literally “bitterness”). Compare מרור : maror.

senses: A garrisoned place, especially one that is or was once under Spanish control.
ety: From Spanish presidio (“garrison”), from Latin praesidium, 1763. Doublet of praesidium and presidium.
